title: A fair procedure in a marriage market

summary.oneLiner: A matching algorithm in which both sides propose each round always yields a stable outcome and, with equal numbers, minimises the worst-off participant's regret.
summary.overview: The standard deferred acceptance (Gale-Shapley) algorithm produces a stable match, one no pair would want to break, but it favours whichever side does the proposing. The authors argue this is a problem where fairness matters, from task-allocation platforms to dating apps. They propose an algorithm in which both sides propose every round and gradually widen their lists, with cycles of mutual proposals settled by a coin flip. It always ends in a stable matching and, when the two sides are equal in size, gives a 'Rawlsian' stable matching that minimises the largest regret any matched person has. It also runs quickly (in polynomial time).
summary.question: Can a matching procedure treat both sides of a two-sided market symmetrically while still guaranteeing a stable outcome that is fair to the worst-off participants?
summary.method: Theoretical algorithm design in the two-sided 'marriage' matching model with strict preferences. The authors define the procedure, check stability against truncated preferences, fall back on an existing random-order mechanism when needed, and prove results on stability, fairness and computing time.
findings: The procedure always ends with a stable matching.
With equal numbers on both sides, the result is a Rawlsian stable matching (it minimises the maximum regret among matched agents); the same holds in markets meeting a 'regularity' condition.
In large markets with unequal sides, the output is Rawlsian with high probability.
It runs in polynomial time, whereas finding the median stable matching is computationally hard.
Unlike deferred acceptance for the proposing side, the procedure is not strategy-proof.
summary.whyItMatters: Platforms that match two sides, such as task-allocation services or dating apps, may care about fairness to both sides and not just stability. The paper offers a fast procedure that aims for the middle of the set of stable matchings rather than one side's favourite.
